title: What Happens When Someone Violates a Family Court Order in Colorado?

content.rendered:
Receiving a court order is often supposed to bring clarity. It may establish parenting time, child support, decision-making responsibilities, or other important parts of your family law case.

But what happens when the other person does not follow it?

It can be incredibly frustrating to have a legally binding court order and still find yourself dealing with missed payments, denied parenting time, or repeated violations. You may feel unsure about what to do next—or whether there is anything you can do at all.

The good news is that you may have options.

A Court Order Is Not Just a Suggestion

A family court order is legally binding, which means both parties are generally expected to follow its terms.

However, not every situation is as simple as one person intentionally refusing to comply. Sometimes, there may be confusion about the order, disagreements about what it means, or circumstances that make compliance more complicated.

That is why it is important to first understand exactly what your order requires and how the other party may be failing to follow it.

Keep Records of What Is Happening

If you believe a court order is not being followed, documentation can be important.

Depending on the situation, it may be helpful to keep records of:

  • Missed child support payments
  • Denied or missed parenting time
  • Messages and communication between both parties
  • Dates and details of specific incidents
  • Any other information related to the violation

Clear and organized records can help you better understand the situation and may be useful if further legal action becomes necessary.

Enforcement May Be an Option

When someone is not following a family court order, there may be legal options available to address the issue.

The appropriate action can depend on the type of order involved and the specific circumstances. In some cases, it may be possible to ask the court to enforce the existing order. In others, additional legal remedies may be available.

The important thing is not to assume that you have to simply accept repeated violations of an existing order.

Avoid Taking Matters Into Your Own Hands

When you feel that the other party is not following the rules, it can be tempting to respond by doing the same. For example, one parent may consider withholding parenting time because child support has not been paid.

However, two separate violations do not necessarily cancel each other out. Taking matters into your own hands can sometimes create additional complications and may affect your own legal position.

Before making decisions that could affect your family law case, it is important to understand your rights and options.

Understanding Your Next Steps

When a court order is not being followed, the situation can feel exhausting—especially when the issue continues over time. Whether you are dealing with unpaid child support, parenting time issues, or another type of violation, understanding your options can help you decide what to do next.

At The Drake Law Firm, we understand how frustrating it can be when an existing court order is not being followed. Our team can help you review your situation, understand the available options, and determine the appropriate next steps based on your circumstances.
